name: Acoustic Modelling for Sets
title: Acoustic Modelling for Sets
answer: Acoustic modelling for sets predicts how sound reflects, absorbs, and diffuses within a designed performance or virtual environment. It covers stage geometry, set materials, audience seating, and moving scenic elements, and it is used to tune loudspeaker placement, verify intelligibility, and previsualize sound for virtual production. The output is typically an impulse response or a real-time spatial audio render that can be auditioned before the set is built.

sections.body: Acoustic modelling for sets predicts how sound reflects, absorbs, and diffuses within a designed performance or virtual environment. It covers stage geometry, set materials, audience seating, and moving scenic elements, and it is used to tune loudspeaker placement, verify intelligibility, and previsualize sound for virtual production. The output is typically an impulse response or a real-time spatial audio render that can be auditioned before the set is built.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard workstation GPUs for interactive previews and on cloud render farms for high-resolution impulse response generation. Real-time systems often use game engines with spatial audio plugins, while offline simulation may use acoustic ray tracing or wave-based solvers. Audio assets and room models are stored alongside the visual set model in a shared production database.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The typical workflow begins with a 3D model of the set, including material assignments for absorption and scattering coefficients. An acoustic solver traces sound paths or solves the wave equation to produce an impulse response for each source and listener position. Machine learning is increasingly used to accelerate these solvers, for example by learning a mapping from geometry and materials to a plausible room response, or to upsample sparse simulation results to full spatial audio.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions center on the set model, the recorded or synthesized impulse responses, and any training data used to teach the acoustic model. If a model is trained on measurements of real venues or on proprietary stage designs, the resulting acoustic predictions may carry licensing or confidentiality obligations. Risk also includes over-reliance on a simulation that misses construction tolerances or audience absorption, so the output is usually validated with on-site measurement before opening.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward real-time, physically informed acoustic rendering that updates as the set changes during rehearsal or live performance. Models are likely to become more tightly coupled with virtual production pipelines, allowing a director to hear a scene from any seat or camera position while the visual set is still being designed. The longer-term goal is a single shared model of the set that serves lighting, sightlines, and sound without separate manual tuning.
